claims.text: Adding 1–2 at% boron during melting will inhibit nucleation and growth of primary crystalline phases in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Boron addition will increase amorphous retention and thermal stability during reheating.
The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy was produced by arc melting.
The alloy exhibits extensive primary non-eutectic crystallization under both slow and rapid cooling.
A small boron addition of about 1–2 at% should be introduced during melting.
Relevant cooling rates span approximately 52 K/s to 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Keeping subsequent reheating below crystallization-onset temperatures ensures preservation of the amorphous structure.
Boron atoms disrupt local atomic ordering and increase packing disorder in this alloy.
Boron reduces atomic diffusivity in this alloy.
Boron interference at potential nucleation sites limits formation of primary crystalline phases.
Retarding atomic mobility and nucleation during cooling and reheating allows the undercooled melt to freeze into a more stable amorphous configuration.
The boron-modified alloy will have a higher amorphous-phase volume fraction than the undoped alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will exhibit a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the undoped alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will have enhanced thermal stability during reheating cycles.
The undoped alloy forms several crystalline phases under slow cooling.
Very rapid melt-spinning at 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbon.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability during very rapid cooling.
Boron will be beneficial throughout the entire cooling-rate range from about 52 K/s to 10^6 K/s.
Processing outside the stated cooling and reheating boundaries may reduce boron's inhibition of crystallization.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant amorphous-fraction increase, an upward crystallization-onset shift, or consistently inhibited nucleation relative to an undoped control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state statement says the alloy exhibits extensive primary crystallization under rapid cooling, whereas the baseline and cited evidence state that very rapid cooling at 10^5–10^6 K/s yields an amorphous structure.

The baseline broadly attributes several crystalline phases to similar cooling conditions, while the proposed boundary includes very rapid cooling for which the undoped alloy is already reported to be amorphous.
Reheating is specified to remain below the known crystallization onset, but measuring and comparing DSC crystallization-onset temperatures ordinarily requires heating through the onset.
